headline_marked: [[Elon Musk to give SpaceX shares]] to kids via Trump Accounts
headline: Elon Musk to give SpaceX shares to kids via Trump Accounts
summary: Musk plans to donate one SpaceX share to "every kid in America" next year, with the distribution to be handled through Trump Accounts.
details: Elon Musk announced plans to donate one share of SpaceX stock to "every kid in America" sometime next year. The initiative will reportedly be facilitated through "Trump Accounts."

The plan was confirmed by Donald Trump on Truth Social, who stated that the shares would be distributed via these accounts. Musk thanked Brad Gerstner, a proponent of Trump Accounts, for his role in enabling the donation.

The value of SpaceX's stock is significant; an estimated 72 million shares would be worth approximately $10.5 billion, according to CNBC. Musk indicated this is just the beginning, stating, "This will be the first of many."

Several prominent figures, including Michael and Susan Dell, Ray and Barbara Dalio, Brad Gerstner, and SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell, have also pledged contributions to Trump Accounts. The White House previously announced that over 70 million such accounts had been created, with 60 million children automatically enrolled in October.

topic: privacy and security concerns with smart home devices and routers
headline_marked: Robot vacuums: [[Your floor maps and data]] could be exposed
headline: Robot vacuums: Your floor maps and data could be exposed
summary: These smart home devices collect more than just dust, potentially revealing sensitive information about your home and habits to manufacturers.
details: Robot vacuums, especially advanced models, can create detailed floor maps, record cleaning histories, and even feature microphones or remote video viewing capabilities. This means they can potentially capture intimate details of your home life, from your daily routines to private moments.

When these devices connect to the cloud, the data they collect is often sent to the manufacturer's servers. While this enables features like remote monitoring, it also raises privacy concerns about who has access to this information and how it's used.

A notable incident involved a security flaw where one user could control thousands of robot vacuums instead of just their own. While the manufacturer patched the issue, it highlighted the underlying security weaknesses in how these devices manage user permissions.

Beyond security breaches, everyday data collection is a concern. Manufacturers like iRobot state that their connected vacuums may share floor maps, room names, detected objects, movement patterns, and even Wi-Fi network details.

To mitigate these risks, consumers should prioritize robot vacuums that minimize data collection, ideally with on-device navigation and processing. Always review the privacy policy before purchasing and be wary of mandatory cloud features.

For those already using a robot vacuum, it's crucial to secure it with a strong password, enable two-factor authentication, and keep firmware updated. Disable remote viewing or other connected features if they make you uncomfortable, unless absolutely necessary.
